newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Diplomats play down delays for new Angolan govt.
newsitem.headline: Diplomats play down delays for new Angolan govt.

text.p: Postponement of the inauguration of Angola's unity government is a temporary hitch and does not mean a breakdown in the peace process to end two decades of civil war, diplomats said on Friday.

"This is not the end of the world. It is important to remember that this government will be in place for at least two years and it has some major responsibilities," said U.S. Ambassador Donald Steinberg, one of three official observers to Angola's peace process.

Angola's ruling MPLA and their former rebel UNITA rivals on Thursday announced the postponement of the inauguration of the country's first united, peace-time government, which had been scheduled for Saturday.
"If it takes another month to ensure UNITA is a full partner, it is a delay worth accepting," Steinberg told Reuters.
The United Nations, overseeing the transformation to peace, said a new date had not yet been set.
Its special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, said he did not believe the delay was serious.
"The process is on course and hopes are still high. There is no impasse as far as I am concerned," he said.
Others involved in the peace process also expressed optimism that the unity government would be formed soon.

"I think it is unfortunate that the date has been delayed, but dates are not important by themselves. If this date is not good for both sides, then let's find another date," said Portugal's Ambassador to Angola Jose Ramello Ortigez.
Western diplomats said the inauguration should follow soon after the arrival in Luanda of 70 UNITA members of parliament, scheduled for February 12.
One official said February 15 was being discussed as a possibility, to coincide with a scheduled trip to South Africa by U.S. Vice-President Al Gore.
But UNITA's peace representative in Luanda, Isaias Samakuva, said he had no information about possible dates.
"I am sure we (UNITA) will propose a date and the government will propose another date and the U.N. will pick a date in the middle that we will end up using," he said.
"I am sure we will come to an agreement..."
The major stumbling block has been defining a role for UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi in the new government.

His party has rejected a vice-presidential post for Savimbi, but after talks with South African President Nelson Mandela earlier this month, the 62-year-old UNITA leader said he would be in the new government to help national reconciliation.
But the government, weary of delays in the implementation of the peace process, accused the former rebels of looking for excuses to set back the formation of the coalition.

"UNITA is just interested in seeking ways to delay the process. We are not at an impasse but this is very bad. We simply cannot continue to go on like this," senior government official Higino Carneiro told reporters.
